interactions.summary: Jiang lands the Yale analogy, briefly jokes with a student about it, and then transitions the class back into the text.

A student reads Beatrice's explanation that the will is God's greatest gift, that a vow binds human consent to divine consent, and that breaking such a pledge cannot simply be compensated by later good action.

claims.claim: In the passage being read, Beatrice says the freedom of the will is God's greatest and most prized gift to rational beings.
The read-aloud passage defines the high worth of a vow by saying that a person pledges free will with consent in a way that counters or meets God's consent.
The quoted argument says that when a path is drawn between a human being and God through vow, the person gives up the treasure of free will to God.
The passage argues that reusing what was already offered to God as compensation would amount to trying to do good by means of ill.
Beatrice's speech, as read here, signals that church dispensation will require more careful explanation because it seems to conflict with the strict logic of vow and free will.

signature_moments.moment: The whole argument is grounded in a single compressed claim: free will is God's greatest gift.
signature_moments.source_phrase: Was the freedom of the will.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the textual hinge for the lecture's whole account of why vows matter so much and why betrayal cannot be erased mechanically.

signature_moments.moment: The read-aloud logic makes compensation paradoxical: to use again what was offered would be trying to do good with ill-gotten means.
signature_moments.source_phrase: seeking to do good with ill
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It gives the sharpest textual statement of why simple repayment cannot reconcile a broken vow.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: In the read-aloud passage, the highest divine gift to beings with intellect and the ground of a vow's seriousness.
A pledge made through consent that joins human consent to God and gives free will over as a treasured offering.

chronology_notes.note: After Jiang's speculative classroom probing, the packet returns to the textual source and grounds the discussion in Beatrice's own logic about free will, vow, and the impossibility of simple compensation.
